primary_cause: Duke announced Mar 19 new COVID-19 customer relief measures — waiving fees suspending disconnections. Not clearly negative. Defensive utilities still being sold for liquidity
secondary_factors: Bad-debt risk and delayed collections as utilities paused shutoffs. Rate-sensitive utilities caught in indiscriminate de-risking
store_description: Duke own March 19 update was operationally supportive not negative which makes this look less like event-driven bad news and more like investors pricing in COVID-related billing stress and forced selling.

primary_cause: Mar 19 Danaher said received FTC clearance for GE Biopharma acquisition ($21.4B requiring divestitures). Despite superficially positive clearance investors focused on transaction execution and balance-sheet risk during global shutdown
secondary_factors: Broad med-tech and life-science tools de-risking. Concern near-term industrial and diagnostics demand harder to forecast
store_description: The only major Danaher-specific news was the final antitrust clearance for the GE Biopharma deal with Danaher still expecting to close by March 31. In calmer markets that likely would have helped but in late March 2020 a large acquisition with financing and integration risk appears to have been treated as a burden.

primary_cause: No clearly negative CVS-specific announcement. Pharmacy and essential retail resilience vs Aetna utilization visibility front-store traffic mix labor costs supply shortages
secondary_factors: General healthcare and consumer de-risking. Investors haircutting mixed pandemic exposures
store_description: CVS was not hit by obvious bad company news. It sat in an awkward middle ground where it benefited from COVID-related demand for health products but faced rising operating complexity and uncertain insurance economics.

primary_cause: Already withdrew Q1 guidance Mar 9 due to worsening COVID travel demand. Border closures and travel restrictions kept intensifying. Collapsing global travel demand
secondary_factors: Mounting border restrictions and air-travel shutdowns made cancellation and refund risk worse
store_description: Booking had already told investors it could no longer stand behind Q1 guidance citing the worsening COVID impact on travel demand. With governments still adding border restrictions and consumers canceling trips the market was repricing BKNG for a deeper and longer travel freeze.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters Mar 17 reported Boeing seeking tens of billions in U.S. government loan guarantees. Boeing backed at least $60B in liquidity support for aerospace industry. Acute liquidity stress and bailout risk
secondary_factors: Aviation demand collapse from COVID. Pre-existing 737 MAX damage
store_description: Boeing issue was not just bad market conditions. By March 17 Reuters was reporting that Boeing needed extraordinary government support and the company soon endorsed a minimum $60B support package for the industry. That signaled a severe liquidity crunch on top of the existing MAX crisis.

primary_cause: No material AMT-specific negative. REIT and liquidity selling. Investors sold liquid winners to raise cash
secondary_factors: Worries that frozen capital market and higher credit spreads could pressure highly valued rate-sensitive REITs even if underlying tower demand stayed solid
store_description: American Tower business was comparatively defensive and no contemporaneous company-specific blowup was found. The most likely explanation is that AMT got dragged down with REITs and other long-duration equities as investors sold liquid winners to raise cash.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Abbott announced Mar 18 received FDA EUA for molecular COVID-19 test — would ship 150,000 tests immediately. Despite positive test news stock sold off on broad med-tech de-risking
secondary_factors: Concern non-COVID procedures and diagnostics would weaken sharply. Investors judged first COVID test launch insufficient to offset looming disruption elsewhere in portfolio
store_description: Abbott actually had good news in the window: FDA authorization and immediate rollout of 150,000 molecular COVID-19 tests. The fact the stock still fell 6.0% suggests the market was looking through that benefit and discounting a much larger pandemic hit to routine medical activity.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Exxon said Mar 16 evaluating significant near-term capex and opex reductions because of COVID and commodity-price declines. Oil-demand collapse plus management explicit acknowledgment spending cuts coming
secondary_factors: Saudi-Russia oil-price war still crushing crude and worsening sector sentiment
store_description: Exxon own March 16 statement told investors that market conditions were bad enough to force significant spending reductions. That was a direct admission that the combination of COVID demand destruction and lower commodity prices was materially impairing the business.

primary_cause: No significant Nvidia-specific negative. Semiconductor de-risking on fears of global demand destruction and supply-chain disruption
secondary_factors: Investors still repricing cyclicals tied to data center gaming consumer electronics and Asian manufacturing exposure
store_description: Nvidia appears to have been hit more by semiconductor and supply-chain fears than by a fresh company-specific headline. In late March 2020 investors were aggressively cutting chip exposure as global lockdowns raised uncertainty around both end-demand and manufacturing continuity.

primary_cause: Mar 16 ServiceNow released four COVID-19 emergency response apps for free. No negative news. High-multiple software de-rating during liquidity panic
secondary_factors: Concern enterprise software deal cycles especially new logo and discretionary workflow projects would slow abruptly
store_description: ServiceNow actually leaned into the crisis with free emergency apps on March 16 which was strategically positive. The 8.3% drop therefore looks like valuation compression in richly valued software names with investors assuming CIOs would pause spending.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Reuters reported Nike closing all stores in U.S. and several other markets. Adidas announced similar closures Mar 17. Direct revenue hit from store closures
secondary_factors: Postponed sporting events. Weaker wholesale demand
store_description: Nike brick-and-mortar footprint was being shut across the U.S. Canada Western Europe Australia and New Zealand directly impairing near-term sales. That was a concrete company-relevant revenue shock not just vague market fear.

primary_cause: No new clearly negative NextEra-specific release. Yieldcos and utilities and renewables sold as funding-sensitive long-duration assets during credit shock
secondary_factors: Investors worried capital-intensive renewables buildouts would become harder to finance if markets stayed stressed. Feb 19 $2.5B equity units sale
store_description: Unlike a plain-vanilla regulated utility NextEra also carried a strong growth-and-financing narrative which became a liability during the cash crunch. With no fresh company-specific bad news the sharp 7.4% decline most likely reflects concern around externally funded growth and valuation compression.

primary_cause: No negative Microsoft-specific release. Windows 10 reached 1B monthly active devices Mar 18. Teams and cloud usage surging. Large-cap tech de-risking
secondary_factors: Concern around LinkedIn ads and transactional licensing as economy froze. Fear of enterprise and SMB spending slowdown
store_description: Microsoft operating news flow was not negative. If anything usage trends were improving as work moved online. The selloff appears driven by investors cutting mega-cap tech exposure and anticipating weaker licensing and advertising demand.

primary_cause: International travel restrictions escalated sharply — U.S.-Canada border measures State Department warning against international travel. Collapse in cross-border and travel-related payment volumes
secondary_factors: Recession fears around consumer spending and merchant volumes. Mastercard later said cross-border metrics had deteriorated further
store_description: Mastercard was especially exposed to the part of payments economics that travel shutdowns destroyed first: high-margin cross-border spending. The market likely sold MA ahead of formal company guidance changes because border closures and international travel warnings were already signaling a severe hit.

primary_cause: No negative Altria-specific headline. FDA authorized IQOS 3 which was positive. Defensive consumer names still being liquidated
secondary_factors: Nicotine and vapor category uncertainty remained background overhang. Recessionary downtrading and retail disruption concerns
store_description: Because there was no obvious bad Altria-specific news immediately before the drop the move looks mostly like investors selling even classic defensives to raise cash. MO also had category-specific uncertainty around reduced-risk products and shifting retail behavior.

primary_cause: No fresh directly negative 3M announcement. Later Apr embroiled in mask and export and price-gouging controversies. Investors focused on broad industrial and cyclical exposure not just N95 upside
secondary_factors: Supply-chain stress. Manufacturing recession risk. Uncertainty whether PPE demand could offset weakness elsewhere
store_description: 3M was a classic mixed-exposure name in March 2020: obvious upside from respirators but large downside risk across industrial electronics transportation and commercial end markets. The 9.2% drop suggests the market decided the non-PPE recession hit would dominate at least near term.

primary_cause: No new negative Mondelez-specific release. Prior disclosure coronavirus hurting operations in China — two factories closed 10 days. Concern global supply-chain and EM exposure would outweigh pantry-loading
secondary_factors: FX and channel-mix worries
store_description: Mondelez was not being sold because of a fresh company bombshell on March 20. More likely investors extrapolated earlier signs of COVID disruption in China to a broader global snack business with factory distribution and currency exposure.

primary_cause: Mar 20 PepsiCo announced enhanced employee benefits and extra frontline compensation. No negative headline. Investors repriced for sharp hit to higher-margin away-from-home channels
secondary_factors: Added labor and operating costs. Broad liquidation of staples. Shutdown of restaurants stadiums workplaces and convenience traffic
store_description: Pepsi March 20 announcement was socially positive but also highlighted rising frontline operating costs. The much more important issue for the stock was probably the shutdown of restaurants stadiums workplaces and convenience traffic which threatened beverage volumes despite stronger pantry demand.

primary_cause: Lam Research issued business update for fiscal quarter ending Mar 29 on Mar 17. Semiconductor equipment names repriced for fab and customer capex risk and supply-chain disruption
secondary_factors: Concern memory and foundry customers would delay spending if pandemic deepened
store_description: Lam did have a COVID-era business update on March 17 which likely reminded investors how exposed wafer-fab equipment is to global supply chains and customer capex cycles. Even without an explicit profit warning the stock decline fits a market aggressively discounting semiconductor-equipment cyclicality.

primary_cause: Mar 20 Lowe's committed $25M and said would reduce store hours starting Mar 23. Rising operating disruption and margin pressure from pandemic response measures
secondary_factors: Uncertainty about store traffic labor availability cleaning and safety costs. Whether home-improvement demand would hold if lockdowns tightened
store_description: Lowe's announcement was not a classic profit warning but it did signal a more expensive and operationally constrained retail environment with reduced hours and additional crisis spending. In late March 2020 the market was still in sell first mode on retailers.
